name: Antimony eyeliner

card.summary: Ground stibnite (antimony sulfide) used since ancient times as black kohl to line and define the eyes, making them appear larger and darker.
card.note: Traditional kohl may contain lead; stibnite is toxic if ingested and the US FDA does not approve kohl as a color additive.

quick.overview:
Antimony eyeliner is kohl made from ground stibnite, a soft grey antimony sulfide mineral. Mixed with fat or other binders and applied along the lash line, it gives a dark, defined eye. People in ancient Egypt and across the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia have used it for centuries.

Beyond appearance, users have credited it with protecting eyes from sun and ailments. Modern products often use soot or other pigments, and the safety of traditional mineral kohl, particularly lead contamination, is the main research topic.
quick.how: The mineral is ground to a fine powder, mixed with fat or another carrier, and drawn along the lash line with a stick or applicator. It is also used to darken brows and lashes.
quick.risks: Stibnite is toxic if ingested, with symptoms resembling arsenic poisoning. Studies have found high lead levels in some commercial kohl, linked to raised blood lead in children, and the US FDA does not approve kohl as a color additive and restricts its import.

lead: Antimony eyeliner is a form of kohl made by grinding stibnite, antimony trisulfide, into a powder applied around the eyes to darken lids and lashes and to define the eye [1][2].

Use dates to around 3000 BCE in the Mediterranean region, and Egyptians of all classes wore kohl, partly for protection from sun and eye ailments [1][2]. Galena (lead sulfide) was also used, and later products may contain it [1].
Research focuses on lead content in commercial kohl and its association with blood lead in children, with some studies disputing the link [1].

chain: Dark mineral powder applied to lash line
Eyes look larger and more defined
angle.text: Black kohl defines the eye line, much like modern eyeliner, and has been used this way for thousands of years.

infobox: Kohl not an approved color additive [1]

paras: Stibnite is a soft grey mineral and the main ore of antimony. Ground and mixed with fat or other binders, it served as an eye cosmetic from about 3000 BCE and also as a medicine in Egypt from the protodynastic period [2]. Egyptian kohl was often galena, applied to the upper lid, with malachite on the lower [1]. Nubian communities also used kohl in the Middle Bronze Age [1].
Kohl remains in use in the Middle East, North Africa, the Horn of Africa and West Africa, and kajal and surma are South Asian relatives [1].

No studies found on stibnite kohl as a cosmetic. Related research covers lead in kohl: studies from the early 1990s found high lead in commercial products and linked contaminated kohl to higher blood lead, though some studies dispute the association, and a 2016 Pakistani study found lead-containing surma a significant exposure source [1]. A 2010 study suggested some ancient lead compounds could boost immune response [1].

Stibnite is toxic if swallowed, with symptoms like arsenic poisoning [2]. The US FDA does not approve kohl as a color additive, considers it unsafe because of possible lead, and bars its import and sale [1].

timeline.event: Antimony sulfide pastes in use as eye cosmetics [2].
Studies report high lead levels in commercial kohl [1].
